args.text:
Take, for example, the business of getting up in the morning. Now, when there's a big house-party it's easy enough, because you can always hear the others padding about and brushing their teeth. You can just time your own getting up by how many people seem to be on the move. But if you're the only guest, there's every chance of a dreadful mix-up.

"What time's brekkie?" you ask.

"Oh, any old time on Sundays," says the hostess, with a big wave of the hand. "Sleep in as long as you like. This is 'Liberty Hall.'"

It's a lovely thought, and nicely meant, but there's nothing in it you can actually get hold of. It does the job at the time, but come the morning it's so vague it's downright terrifying.

Say you wake up at eight. You listen and can't hear a soul. So it's back over onto the cool pillow till eight-twenty. Then up on the elbow again, head cocked to one side. There's a creak somewhere near the stairs. They might all be up and heading down to breakfast! It takes about two seconds to leap out of bed and listen at the door. Maybe open it, ever so politely, and have a peek out. Dead silence, broken only, as they say, by the ticking of the hall clock, and not a soul about. They must be late sleepers. Maybe eleven o'clock is their Sunday getting-up time. Some people _are_ like that. Too right they are.

Shut the door and sit on the edge of the bed. Going back to sleep is out of the question now. Let's have a squiz at the pictures in the guest-room, just to kill a bit of time. Here's one of Lorna Doone. How d'e do, Lorna? Here's a group shot--taken in 1902--of your host in evening clothes, holding a mandolin. Probably in the musical club at his college. Bit of a scruffy-looking lot, you _have_ to say. Well, what about this one? An etching of some dodgy-looking barges on what's probably the Thames. Not bad, I s'pose.

Back to the door to listen again. Tick-tock-tick-tock. If you ran yourself a bath you'd probably wake the whole house. Better sit back down on the edge of the bed.

Hello, there are some books on the table. "Fifty Famous Sonnets," illustrated by Maxfield Parrish. Never touch a sonnet before breakfast. "My experiences in the Alps," by a lady mountain-climber who's written on the fly-leaf, "To my good friends the Elbridges, in memory of many happy days together at Chamounix. October, 1907." Well, that's _that_ sorted. "Essay on Compensation" in limp leather, by R.W. Emerson, published by Houghton, Mifflin & Co. Oh, all right then! Reckon they thought that'd be over your head, did they? Well, we'll show 'em! We'll read it just to spite 'em. Opening it at the red ribbon:

"Of the like nature is that expectation of change which instantly follows the suspension of our voluntary activity. The terror of cloudless noon--"

Hang on, it must be nearly noon by now! Ten past nine, that's all! Well, the only thing for it is to get dressed and go out for a wander round the grounds. Forget the bath, it's too noisy. And so, very carefully, almost on the sly, you get yourself dressed.
